title: Greetings and introductions
goal: Greet people, introduce yourself, and say goodbye with the words Sundanese people actually use — and meet, for the first time, the two speech levels that run through this whole course.
bekal: greet people by time of day and by who you are talking to
introduce yourself with *abdi*, not *kuring*, and understand why
use the three words that change how Sundanese people treat you: *punten*, *mangga*, *hatur nuhun*

dialogs.title: Paguneman — At the boarding-house door
dialogs.intro: Rani's first evening in Bandung. She is standing at the door of a *kosan* (a boarding house that rents rooms) in a narrow lane in Dago, dragging two suitcases. A middle-aged woman opens the door.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Mangga, mangga. Neng anu badé ngontrak téh?
lines.id: Come in, come in. So you're the one who's renting the room?
lines.literal: please, please. Néng who will rent [téh]?

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Yes, ma'am. My name is Rani.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Wilujeng sumping, Néng Rani. Abdi Bu Imas. Kumaha damang?
lines.id: Welcome, Rani. I'm Bu Imas. How are you?
lines.literal: welcome, Néng Rani. I Bu Imas. how healthy?

lines.id: Fine, thank God, ma'am. And you?

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.id: Fine, thanks to your good wishes. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Oh, pantes. Tiasa basa Sunda henteu?

lines.literal: oh, no-wonder. can language Sundanese not?

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: A little, ma'am. I've only just started learning.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Sae atuh. Engké ku Ibu diajarkeun. Mangga lebet heula.
lines.id: Well, good for you. I'll teach you. Come on in first.

lines.id: No problem at all. I hope you'll feel at home here.

notes: **Punten** is the most important word in this course, and you should be using it before you finish Unit 1. It means "excuse me", but it covers far more ground: knocking on a door, passing in front of someone who is seated, interrupting, apologizing lightly, and opening a question to a stranger. The answer is almost always **mangga**. In Bandung, walking past people without saying *punten* looks rude — not slightly rude, genuinely rude.

**Mangga** means **please, go ahead**, and has nothing to do with the fruit (*mangga* is "mango" in Indonesian). It answers *punten*, and it also invites someone to come in, sit down, eat, or go first. Say it *mahng-GAH*, with the stress at the end. The very polite form is *sumangga*.

**Hatur nuhun** = thank you. The short, casual form is **nuhun**; the most polite is **hatur nuhun pisan**. The reply is *sami-sami* (you're welcome) or, casually, just *heueuh*. ⚠️ Don't answer with *mangga* — that is the reply to *punten*, not to thanks.

**Kumaha damang?** = "how are you?" in lemes (polite) Sundanese, literally "how, healthy?". The standard answer is **damang** or **pangéstu, damang** — "thanks to your blessing, healthy". That *pangéstu* reply feels very Sundanese: your good health is credited to the other person's prayers. In loma (casual) speech people ask *kumaha kabarna?* and answer *sae* or *alus*.
**Muhun** = yes (polite). The casual form is **heueuh**, said *heu-euh* in two dull beats. Indonesian *iya* is also heard, but *muhun* sits much better with older people.

**Nembé** = just now, only just started (lemes; the loma form is *kakara*). *Abdi nembé diajar* ("I've only just started learning") is a lifesaver you will use dozens of times this month — it makes people slow down at once.

**Néng, Aa, Téh, Mang, Bi** are terms of address that replace "you". *Néng* for a young woman, *Aa* for a man a little older than you, *Téh* (from *Teteh*) for a woman a little older, *Mang* (from *Emang*) for a man of an uncle's age, *Bi* (from *Bibi*) for a woman of an aunt's age. Using a term of address is always safer than using a pronoun.

grammars.title: Two speech levels — a first look
body: *Nami abdi Rani* and *Ngaran kuring Rani* mean exactly the same thing: "my name is Rani". What differs is not the meaning but **who** you are allowed to say it to.
Sundanese has two basic speech levels, and almost every everyday word has two forms:

head: Meaning
Loma (casual)
Lemes (polite)
Used with
rows: loma: friends your own age · lemes: anyone you respect

after: For a newcomer, one rule is enough: **use lemes with everyone until you are genuinely close.** Speaking too politely to a friend your age just makes you sound a bit over-polite — it offends no one. Speaking loma to an older person sounds rude, and Sundanese people usually won't correct you; they will simply keep their distance.

⚠️ There is a third set of words you must **never** use about yourself; Unit 3 covers it in full. For now, remember one example: *tuang* (eat) is never used for yourself. *Abdi badé tuang* ("I am going to dine", with the honorific verb) is the most famous newcomer mistake.

These two levels are not a stiff palace etiquette like court Javanese. In everyday Bandung conversation people switch between them within one chat — polite to an older passer-by, casual to the friend next to them, then polite again. That ability to switch is what this course trains.

blocks.text: Sundanese time-of-day greetings start with **wilujeng** ("good…", literally "safe, blessed"), and the day is divided a little differently from English:

head: Greeting
When
Notes
rows: = congratulations, in the sense of giving thanks

blocks.text: In casual conversation, time-of-day greetings are rare. What you really hear in the lanes, at food stalls, and on campus are opening questions:

items: **Kumaha damang?** — how are you? (lemes). Answer: *damang* / *pangéstu, damang* / *alhamdulillah, damang*.
**Kumaha kabarna?** — how are things? (loma). Answer: *sae* / *alus* / *biasa waé*.
**Badé ka mana?** — where are you off to? (lemes). ⚠️ This is a **greeting**, not an interrogation. The safest answer: *badé ka payun* ("just up ahead") — as vague as "oh, just out" in English.
**Ti mana?** — where have you been? A throwaway answer like *ti bumi* (from home) is enough.
**Tos tuang?** — have you eaten? A very common greeting, especially around midday. ⚠️ For other people use *tuang*; when answering about yourself use *neda*: *Tos, hatur nuhun.*

blocks.title: Saying goodbye
items: **Amit mundur** — excuse me, I'll take my leave. The most polite form, used when leaving someone's home.
**Amit, Bu / Amit, Pa** — the short form, safe anywhere.
**Wilujeng angkat** — to someone who is **leaving** (= have a safe trip).
**Wilujeng kantun** — to someone who is **staying behind** (= goodbye).
**Dugi ka énjing** — see you tomorrow. **Dugi ka pendak deui** — see you again.
**Ati-ati di jalan** — take care on the way. Used just like "drive safely".

blocks.text: Sundanese word order here is simple and close to English: subject first, no verb "to be" needed. What changes is the vocabulary — and the choice of speech level:

head: Basa Sunda (lemes)
English
Loma form
rows: Umur kuring dua puluh lima taun.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Watch out for **urang**. It has two meanings, both common: *urang Sunda* = a Sundanese person, but *urang balik yu* = "let's go home" (*urang* = we). Context always makes it clear, but don't be surprised when the same word turns up as "we".

The most useful habit to copy: with people you don't know, **the pronoun is usually dropped and replaced by a term of address**. Not *Anjeun ti mana?* but *Ibu ti mana?* ("Where is Ma'am from?"); not *Anjeun badé ka mana?* but *Aa badé ka mana?*. It is like saying "Is Sir ready to order?" — except that in Sundanese it is completely normal.

head: Term of address
For whom
Example
rows: man a little older than you
woman a little older than you

blocks.title: Lifesaver sentences for Unit 1
items: **Punten, abdi nembé diajar basa Sunda.** — Sorry, I've only just started learning Sundanese.
**Hapunten, abdi teu ngartos.** — Sorry, I don't understand.
**Tiasa langkung lalaunan?** — Could you speak more slowly?
**Dina basa Sunda, kumaha nyebatna?** — How do you say it in Sundanese?
